text:
None of the four hypotheses is supported by the abstract, so I reject all of them.

**Hypothesis 1** proposes TiO2 nanoparticles whose thermal conductivity adapts from 0.15 to 0.45 W/mK over 35–85 °C. The abstract never mentions TiO2, and it reports no temperature-dependent conductivity behaviour. Its only conductivity-related result is a 145.06% gain in convective heat transfer coefficient from carbon nanotubes in normal saline.

**Hypothesis 2** combines electrostatic atomization, SiO2 at 2% (w/v), 10% (v/v) magnetorheological fluid, and specific thresholds (≥40% tool wear reduction, ≥30% Ra improvement). The abstract mentions none of SiO2, MR fluid, or these thresholds. Its quantitative results involve jatropha oil-based alumina (85% friction coefficient reduction) and alumina cutting fluid in hard milling (177–230% tool life improvement). It does discuss atomization mechanisms and supply equipment in general terms, but that does not support the specific claims.

**Hypothesis 3** claims electrostatic atomization with a SiO2 biolubricant reduces friction by at least 30% and wear by at least 25%. The abstract reports no SiO2 biolubricant result and no electrostatic-specific finding. Its friction figure (85%) concerns alumina in jatropha oil and is not comparable to the claimed 30%.

**Hypothesis 4** describes a CuO nanofluid whose concentration is actively adjusted from real-time temperature and vibration data, with improvements of at least 20% tool wear, 15% surface finish and 10% specific cutting energy on AISI 1045 and AlSi10Mg. The abstract mentions none of CuO, real-time closed-loop control, vibration sensing, or those specific materials. It does note a "parameterized controllable supply system" and the mapping between nanofluid parameters and machining performance, but a review describing a controllable supply system does not establish dynamic concentration modulation or these quantitative gains.

VERDICT 1: REJECT
VERDICT 2: REJECT
VERDICT 3: REJECT
VERDICT 4: REJECT
